The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(N=2100\). For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(n)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(n\).

Replacing \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) replaces the pair of \(p\)-exponents \((v_p(a),v_p(b))\) by  
\((\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\max(v_p(a),v_p(b)))\).  
Thus, for every prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-exponents on the board is invariant.

When the process stops, no pair of numbers can be incomparable under divisibility; otherwise replacing them would change the board. Therefore the final numbers, sorted as

\[
x_1\le x_2\le \cdots \le x_{2100},
\]

form a divisibility chain:

\[
x_1\mid x_2\mid \cdots \mid x_{2100}.
\]

For each prime \(p\), the exponents \(v_p(x_i)\) are nondecreasing in \(i\), and since the multiset of \(p\)-exponents is invariant, \(v_p(x_i)\) must be the \(i\)-th smallest value among the initial exponents \(v_p(1),\dots,v_p(2100)\).

We need \(x_{2026}\). This is the \(2100-2026+1=75\)-th largest entry in the final chain. Hence its \(p\)-exponent is the largest \(e\) such that at least \(75\) of the original numbers are divisible by \(p^e\).

The number of integers \(n\le 2100\) divisible by \(p^e\) is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^e}\right\rfloor.
\]

So the exponent of \(p\) in \(x_{2026}\) is

\[
e_p=\max\left\{e:\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^e}\right\rfloor\ge 75\right\}.
\]

Since \(2100/75=28\), this is equivalent to

\[
p^e\le 28.
\]

Thus:

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
p & 2 & 3 & 5 & 7 & 11 & 13 & 17 & 19 & 23 & \ge 29\\
\hline
e_p & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\]

Therefore

\[
x_{2026}=2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

The number of positive divisors is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2^6
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
